newsitem.title: USA: U.S. report on Nazi gold will pull no punches.
newsitem.headline: U.S. report on Nazi gold will pull no punches.

text.p: U.S. Under Secretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat told thousands of Holocaust survivors on Sunday that a U. S. government report to be released this week on the Nazi gold looted from victims during the Second World War will pull no punches.

"Our report is not a political document. It is an historian report. It will be over 200 pages with 200 documents to buttress our findings so that they will stand up even in a court of law," Eizenstat told more than 3,000 people at the Fifth Avenue Temple Emanu-el in Manhattan who attended the largest Holocaust Memorial program in the United States.
"This report will be objective. It will be fair and it will be tough in not only revealing the role of the neutrals but also shining the spotlight on the U.S. government. It will pull no punches."

The report, based on 14 million pages of U.S. government documents, was prepared under the direction of Eizenstat. It is expected to be released on Wednesday, and sources close to the State Department said it would be very harsh on the Swiss role in the war as bankers and even money-launderers for the Third Reich.
Eizenstat has played a key role in negotiating the return of properties confiscated from Jewish victims of Nazi Germany to Holocaust survivors and their families.

Although Eizenstat did not go into details of the report he did say that it was impossible to escape the conclusion even after the war, "that the primary victims were the victims--You the survivors. You have suffered so much and gotten back so little."

Alfonse D'Amato, the New York Republican Senator joined with other dignitaries and survivors of Nazi concentration camps, members of resistance groups and their families at the temple to honor the memory of the six million Jews who died at the hands of the Nazi.

After the memorial observance, D'Amato said that the report would shed some light on what happened to the gold of Holocaust victims and also that "this country did not do what they should have done." He did not elaborate.

During the two hour Holocaust Remembrance Day commemoration, women survivors of the Holocaust and children of survivors lit candles in memory of their loved ones. Similar memorials were held in 230 communities in the United States including a ceremony at the Capitol in Washington.
